problem: ObjectNav methods learn 'where to look' for an unseen object through interactive RL. This holds both for end-to-end RL (DD-PPO, Red-Rabbit, THDA) and for modular RL such as SemExp's long-term-goal policy. These methods need large compute (~8 GPUs for days; up to thousands of GPU-hours), are sample-inefficient, and generalize poorly to new scenes.
motivation: Modular pipelines already separate 'where to look?' from 'how to navigate to (x,y)?'. However, the high-level goal selector is still trained with reward-based RL, and the reward is built from the same 3D semantic annotations. The authors hypothesize that 'where to look?' is a perception problem. If so, it can be learned by supervised prediction on a passive dataset of top-down semantic maps, with no environment interaction at all.
key_idea: Train a UNet to predict two frontier-defined potential functions from a partial semantic map, using only offline top-down maps from 3D annotations. The area potential measures unexplored free space beyond each frontier; the object potential is a normalized geodesic distance to the goal category. At test time the agent navigates to the argmax of their average.
insight: Predicting potential functions beats directly predicting where the object is, even with the same data and encoder. On Gibson val, PONI reaches 73.6 SR / 41.0 SPL vs 69.9/35.7 for Predict-θ and 66.9/34.2 for Predict-xy; imitation of actions (BC 12.2 SR, Predict-A 14.7 SR) fails badly. The Tab. 3 ablation shows that exploration carries most of the performance. On Gibson, dropping the area PF (Uo + F-only) cuts SR to 65.1, while dropping the object PF (F-only + Ua) only cuts it to 72.7. Defining potentials only at frontiers helps (Uo alone 58.8 → 65.1 SR). The object PF's influence rises late in episodes (Fig. S1). The main error source is perception rather than search: GT segmentation lifts MP3D SR from 31.8 to 58.2, while the SPL/Success ratio drops only 6–19% without it.
method: Semantic mapper (from SemExp): depth → point cloud registered with the odometry pose, each point labeled by Mask R-CNN (Gibson, COCO-pretrained and fine-tuned on 15 categories) or RedNet (MP3D, 21 categories, trained by THDA), then projected into an (N+2)×M×M allocentric map (obstacle, explored, N object channels).

Potential function network: UNet encoder with 4 downsampling blocks and two UNet decoders with sigmoid outputs. The area decoder outputs a 1-channel area PF; the object decoder outputs an N-channel object PF, one channel per category, and the goal channel is selected at test time.

Area potential U^a: unexplored free-space cells on the complete map are grouped into connected components (OpenCV). A component is linked to a frontier if it is 8-connected-adjacent to it. A frontier's value is the summed area of its linked components, normalized by total free space (a fixed constant on MP3D). Non-frontier pixels are 0.

Object potential U^o(o,x) = max(1 − d_g(o,x)/d_max, 0): d_g is the geodesic distance from frontier x to the 1.0 m success zone of the nearest instance of category o, computed on the complete map; d_max is chosen on validation.

Interaction-free dataset: per-floor semantic maps are projected from 3D annotations using Semantic MapNet code, with floors split by DBSCAN on navigable-point heights, then randomly translated and rotated. Partial maps come from revealing 3m×3m squares along a shortest path between two random free points. This yields 400k training / 1k val tuples per dataset. Training uses MSE restricted to frontier pixels (L = La + Lc), Adam at lr 1e-3, 3 epochs.

Long-term goal selection: U = αU^a + (1−α)U^o with α = 0.5. Explored non-frontier cells are zeroed; predictions in unexplored cells are kept to tolerate noisy frontiers. The argmax is the goal, re-sampled every step (T=1, vs T=25 in prior modular methods).

Analytical local policy: the Fast Marching Method on the obstacle channel gives a shortest path to the long-term goal. The agent follows it with deterministic discrete actions and stops once the goal object is detected in the semantic map (same local policy/stopping as SemExp).

setting.backbone: UNet encoder-decoder potential function network (trained from scratch, supervised). Segmentation: COCO-pretrained Mask R-CNN fine-tuned on Gibson (Gibson) / RedNet trained by THDA (MP3D). Analytical FMM local planner.
setting.training_data: No environment interaction. Offline top-down semantic maps from 3D semantic annotations: 63 train / 13 val per-floor maps (Gibson tiny) and 153 train / 21 val (MP3D). From these, 400,000 train / 1,000 val (partial map, area PF, object PF) tuples per dataset are generated, with random translation/rotation augmentation; 3 epochs. The Gibson segmenter is fine-tuned on Gibson tiny train images.
setting.observation: egocentric 640×480 RGB-D + (x,y,θ) odometry (noise-free in sim), goal category
setting.action_space: discrete move_forward / turn_left / turn_right / stop, driven by argmax long-term goal on the map + FMM planner
setting.privileged: none for main method (noise-free depth/pose as in the Habitat 2021 challenge). A 'GT' ablation uses ground-truth semantic segmentation (marked privileged).

The training-cost comparison (7× vs SemExp, 1,600× vs THDA) is given only as a plot in Fig. 4.
results: On Gibson val, PONI reaches 73.6 SR / 41.0 SPL / 1.25 DTS, beating the SoTA modular RL method SemExp (71.7/39.6/1.39) at 7× lower training cost. On MP3D val it gets 31.8 SR / 12.1 SPL, above THDA (28.4/11.0) at 1,600× lower training cost. Red-Rabbit has higher SR on MP3D val (34.6) but much lower SPL (7.9). On the Habitat 2021 test-standard leaderboard PONI is best among published methods on 3 of 4 metrics: SPL 8.82, SoftSPL 17.08, DTS 8.68. Its success (20.01) is below THDA (21.08) and Red-Rabbit (23.67).
limitations: Success and stopping depend entirely on the semantic map built from image segmentation, with no mechanism to handle segmentation errors. Removing GT segmentation cuts SR by 14.9% (Gibson) and 45.4% (MP3D) relative.
Training requires human-annotated 3D semantic scene annotations to build the map dataset, unlike self-supervised alternatives.
Evaluated only in simulation with noise-free depth and pose, with no real-robot experiment. MP3D absolute performance stays low (31.8 SR val, 20.01 test).
